paper_title: Halley: A Predictive Control Plane for Optical AI Data Center Networks

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A frontier AI model is trained in an AI data center, on tens of thousands of accelerators joined by a dedicated network, and every training step ends with all of them exchanging data at once. Between racks, that network is optical, and each of its four layers, from lasers to switches, runs a fixed or after-the-fact policy. Lasers sharing an enclosure, cooling, and power can fail together. At a fixed spare ratio, correlated failure provably caps a pool's availability however large it grows. In this paper, we present a comprehensive predictive control plane framework, called Halley, that reads each resource's next state and acts before the failure occurs. It has four components, each carrying a formal guarantee: LightReserve that sizes the laser pool to provide a coverage bound, FoldFit that schedules the switch within $11/9$ of the optimal, ThermaLead that holds a microring with one-step-ahead control, and TriageGuard that protects the highest-risk modules first. Halley gives each layer a predictive controller that defers to the deployed policy when unsure. Composed from simulations at that point, effective goodput, the share of ideal throughput kept, rises from 65.2\% to 76.5\% if a window that exhausts its spares is lost. If only the dark channels' bandwidth is lost, it reaches 67.4\%. Per megawatt, that is up to 1.03--1.17 times the training; for the same training, up to 3.3--14.7\% less data center capacity. \textsf{Halley}'s fallback circuits are formally verified and are shown to achieve close timing on a commercial FPGA, and pass a 130~nm signoff.

Index TermsCo-packaged optics, common-cause failure, data center networks, distributed training, microring modulators, optical circuit switching, optical interconnects, predictive control, reliability I. INTRODUCTION frontier AI training run usually occupies single cluster in an AI data center, where dedicated network moves data among tens of thousands of accelerators. Between racks, copper cannot carry that data within its power and reach budget, so the network is optical [1], and the industry is now moving the optics onto the package itself, next to the switch or accelerator silicon, an arrangement known as co-packaged optics (CPO). This network, the fabric, has an optical data plane of four layers, each managed on its own today. shared pool of external lasers supplies light to many photonic engines, the on-package optical transceivers of CPO. An optical circuit switch (OCS) joins those engines to one another by connecting whole light paths instead of forwarding individual packets. Microring modulators, ring resonators few microns in radius, encode the data onto each wavelength. The lasers arrive in field-replaceable modules that are swapped in service. At hundred-thousand-accelerator scale, reliability, network topology, and checkpointing have become first-order design constraints [1]. Each layer faces an online allocation decision under hard service constraint: how many spare lasers the pool should hold, which circuits the switch should hold and for how long, where each rings heater should be set, and which modules receive the few hot spares, each wired to its module in advance. The deployed policies this paper replaces, which we call reactive for short, either fix each answer once in advance or make it only after the event it should have anticipated. Training is bulk-synchronous: every training step ends in collective, phase in which all accelerators communicate at once and which also acts as barrier, so the step finishes only when its slowest link does. drifted ring, failed laser, or late switch reconfiguration therefore leaves every accelerator idle at that barrier. Software-defined networking provisioned for separate control plane from the data plane. Production optical fabrics use that approach for provisioning. For example, Googles Jupiter fabric routes on predicted traffic matrix [2] and TPUv4 reconfigures its optical circuit switches to ride through outages [3], [4]. Similarly, Ironwood TPUs 9,216-chip superpods use them to route around interruptions, the MixNet research system reconfigures ahead of predicted all-to-all [5]. The Opus system reconfigures photonic rails at the boundaries between parallelism phases [6]. Failure prediction for pluggable optical transceivers is now validated on production data [7], [8]. We observed that existing control planes do not forecast the copackaged optical hardware itself, lasers failure or rings drift, and hence do not act before the failure or drift arrives. Proposed Halley framework: This work presents Halley, control plane that provides these necessary features. The system has multiple components as described below. The Halley framework provides every layer with component of its own. LightReserve sizes the laser pool to coverage bound instead of fixed ratio: floor on the chance that its spares absorb every failure in window, valid for the assumed failure rate and correlation. FoldFit schedules the OCS so that, under stated conditions, schedules total dwell time, the time its circuits are held, stays within 11/9 of the shortest possible, bound that leaves out switching delay. ThermaLead sets each microrings heater ahead of the drift. TriageGuard steers limited budget of hot spares to the modules most likely to fail. Each component predicts its layers next state and acts 2 before it arrives. Each steps aside to the reactive system that it replaces when its forecast is stale or unsure. Hence, for such forecast the result is no worse than current systems, though confident but wrong forecast has no such floor yet. Adding spares is the usual way to keep shared laser pool lit. In co-packaged pool the lasers are unlikely to fail independently. NVIDIAs external laser module holds eight lasers in one temperature-controlled enclosure [9]. Hence, the lasers of module share its heat and often one power supply, and thermal or power fault that stresses one laser stresses its neighbors as well. Failures that arrive together can exhaust the spares. Growing the pool at the same spare ratio, the share of the pool held as spares, does not spread that risk away, since the next burst of failures is correlated too. At fixed spare ratio, availability converges as the pool grows to closed-form ceiling < 1 that depends on the failure correlation ρ and the per-laser failure probability but not on the pools size. Raising the spare ratio does lift availability, but past certain point so slowly that high target needs pool larger than any operator would deploy. The limit itself is classical. When exchangeable failures are positively correlated, the failed fraction of large pool converges to random level instead of to its mean [10]. Common-cause models in reliability engineering bound redundant systems the same way [11], [12]. What this paper adds is its consequence for pooled laser supply: where the cap binds, what it costs in spares, and the cheaper alternative. However, correlation can be controlled. Separating the lasers into distinct thermal and power domains and sourcing them from diverse batches raises the ceiling, which redundancy cannot. Technical contributions: The main contributions are: First, it carries the classical exchangeable limit over to pooled laser supplies and proves that in pool of many modules the correlation between modules, more than within them, sets the cap. Under stated cost model, it also finds that decorrelating before buying spares is the cheaper path across the range of correlations considered plausible. Second, it builds the proposed Halley control plane framework, that has four major components. Three of its four components carry formal guarantee, stated in idealized form later. The novel aspect is the design for the failure physics of the AI data center. Third, it composes the components into effective cluster goodput under two readings of spare shortfall, couples the laser and thermal losses through shared common cause, reports the tail as well as the mean, and proves closed form for the correlation-driven part of that tail. Fourth, it synthesizes, places, and routes the fallback circuits for commercial field-programmable gate array, carries the same sources through signoff as SkyWater 130 nm layout, and formally verifies their register-transfer design, the part of Halley that can be built today. The paper also reports detailed performance study of the proposed mechanisms, based on simulation and mathematical modeling, and their circuit-level realization: an FPGA build and signed-off SkyWater 130 nm layout. The software implementation of these components and the hardware design are available at [13]. Important Results: At the correlation we assume for wellbuilt package and the stress failure rate of Section III-III-B, pool with one spare per active laser, the 2 budget cap we assume throughout, cannot pass 99.670% availability however large it grows. reserve of four spares for 32 channels, the proportion an analyst reports for related shipping part, reaches only 86.3%. Availability of 99.999% is then out of reach for any spare ratio within that cap. For 32-channel pool at that correlation, 99.999% stays out of reach within the 2 cap whenever lasers failure probability per restock window exceeds about 2.4 104. At 50 failures per billion hours (50 FIT), the Optical Internetworking Forum (OIF) target for laser source, which we apply to each laser, laser crosses that probability once the restock window exceeds about 200 days. With the spare count held at the 23 lasers our sizing rule returns for 99% target, cutting the correlation from ρ = 0.15 to ρ = 0.03 moves availability from about 99% to just past 99.999%. Under stated cost model at the stress rate, reaching 99.999% by separating the pool first and then sizing its spares costs $44,100 in all, against $234,000 for spares alone. The overall figure of merit is effective cluster goodput, defined as the fraction of the clusters ideal throughput that survives the losses of the fabric. At the stress setting, composing the simulated components lifts it from 65.2% to 76.5%, 17.3% relative gain. That figure counts every window whose failures exhaust the spares as lost, which we call the coverage reading. On the lit-share reading, in which only the dark channels bandwidth is lost, goodput rises from the same 65.2% baseline to just 67.4%. Most of the gain thus comes from provisioning decision: the larger spare pool that LightReserve sizes for the correlation static reserve ignores. Holding that pool to the 2 cap costs only 0.2 points, and where no spare count within the cap reaches target, LightReserve determines the decorrelation it needs. ThermaLeads simple forecast does slightly worse than the deployed dither lock on the stress trace; gated to fall back to that lock whenever its recent error is the larger of the two, it has 2.1% fewer lock losses. At 50 FIT and 90-day restock the fixed reserve already covers nearly every window, so the composed relative gain falls to about 1.3%; with yearly restocks, 99.999% still exceeds the 2 cap at 50 FIT. Within each reading, the stress-case gain is an upper bound on the useful compute freed from the same silicon and power, because it treats fabric stall as the only recoverable loss. This bound matters because power and local approval now limit how fast new AI data centers are built. new grid connection can take five to ten years [14]. Around 45 US data center projects worth $68 billion were blocked or delayed at the local level between April and June 2026 [15]. Every point of goodput that the fabric loses is capacity that was built and powered but did no useful work. At the bound, what Halley recovers means up to 14.7% fewer new megawatts to site and connect for given training target, or up to 1.17 times as much training from the power already in place, with no wait for new grid connection. On the lit-share reading the figures are 3.3% and 1.03 times. Energy per unit of training falls too, though by less, since waiting accelerator draws less than full power. 3 Fig. 1. The CPO data plane. Top: its four layers, each with the decision it must make and the policy deployed today. Bottom: the light path. External laser modules supply light to each photonic engine, microring modulators in the engine encode data onto it, and the OCS switches the modulated signals between engines [schematic]. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the background material and related work. Section III presents the impact of failure correlation on various metrics such as availability. Section IV presents the control plane framework and the four mechanisms proposed in this paper. Section presents detailed performance study of the proposed mechanisms based on simulation and mathematical modeling studies. Section VI presents the circuit-level realization of the proposed mechanisms, built for commercial FPGA and signed off as SkyWater 130 nm layout. Section VII presents detailed discussion of the proposed framework including its limitations. Section VIII concludes the paper. II. BACKGROUND

sections.title: This section presents the relevant background and related
sections.content: material. A. Data Center Networks The fabric is kept separate from the general-purpose frontend network, and purpose-built production fabrics such as Alibabas High Performance Network (HPN) have moved far from the classical data center architecture [16]. 1) Optical Networking: Optics replaces wiring problem with an allocation problem at two levels: inside single link and across the fabric that joins the links. Inside link, wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) multiplies capacity without adding cable, because each channel travels on its own wavelength, and that makes capacity allocation scheduling problem: which transmitter sends on which wavelength, and when. The problem has long literature on star-coupled and mesh WDM networks, covering prediction-based and intervalbased schedulers [17][19] and restoration mechanisms for channel and link failures [20], [21]. The same problem recurs across the fabric in optical circuit switching. An OCS passes the signal through untouched at any line rate, but demand shifts, so scheduler must break the demand matrix, the traffic each endpoint must send to each other endpoint, into sequence of switch configurations. 2) Training Traffic: Data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism split training job across the accelerators. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models add expert parallelism, which spreads specialist the experts, across the jobs worker parts of the model, processes and routes each token to few of them [5], [22]. Expert dispatch is an all-to-all collective. Its demand matrix is dense within each expert group and sparse across groups, and it shifts as some experts draw more tokens than others. FoldFit schedules these matrices in Section IV. Published runs show the scale: Llama 3 was trained on about 16,000 GPUs [23], MegaScale scaled training past 10,000 [24], DeepSeek-V3 used 2,048 [25], and Meta reports training on the order of 100,000 GPUs [26]. At this scale hardware is the main threat. Llama 3 attributed about 78% of its unexpected interruptions to confirmed or suspected hardware issues [23]. study of two large research clusters reports mean time to failure of 7.9 hours for 1,024-GPU jobs; InfiniBand link failures were among the top causes of job failures, and most of those came in one short burst from handful of nodes [27]. Metas report on 32,000-GPU job counts 2.3 interruptions per 1,000 servers per day, 78% of them hardware-related, and Meta estimates one failure every 18 minutes at 100,000 GPUs [26]. B. Optical Data Plane in Data Center Network Fig. 1 shows the four optical layers of the data plane. a) The CPO data plane: CPO moves the photonic engines from the rack edge onto the switch or accelerator package, and the light source changes with them: shared pool of external lasers, in field-replaceable modules, replaces one laser per engine. Each NVIDIA Quantum-X package uses 18 photonic engines fed by 36 laser inputs [28]. The light comes from external laser modules of eight lasers each, and one module powers 32 of the switchs 576 transmit lanes [9], which implies 18 modules and 144 lasers per switch; the 36 laser inputs above describe single package. The OIF implementation agreement for external laser modules, the external laser small form-factor pluggable (ELSFP), allows an optional thermoelectric cooler and replacement at the faceplate [29]. An analyst reports that each related Spectrum-X package carries 36 photonic engines, 32 active and four held in reserve for redundancy [28]; NVIDIAs own description of the single-ASIC version lists 32 engines fed by 16 laser modules and mentions no reserve [9]. 4 We apply that proportion of engines to the laser pool, so 32 active channels backed by four-laser reserve is this papers calibration point throughout, and every later use of the four-laser reserve rests on this assumption. Other vendors also use external lasers. Broadcoms Tomahawk 6-Davisson, sampling since October 2025, places 102.4 Tb/s of CPO behind field-replaceable ELSFP laser modules. Light sources are also changing form. Lightmatters Guide is one-rack-unit light engine whose output would otherwise take about 18 ELSFP modules [30]. Lumentum has announced an eight-wavelength dense-WDM ELSFP with initial availability in the first half of 2027 [31]. How many lasers share an enclosure, the grouping behind the module-level correlation of Section V-V-A, therefore varies by design. The alternative keeps the optics in pluggable module that can be serviced on its own. Mesh Opticals linearpluggable optics drop the digital signal processor that retimes and equalizes the signal, and the vendor reports draw under 10 watts at 1.6 Tb/s [32]. NVIDIA, which reported Spectrum-X Photonics in full production in June 2026, presents it as giving five times the power efficiency and five times the AI uptime of networks built on pluggable transceivers [33]. b) Optical circuit switching and MoE traffic: Jupiter brought optical circuit switching to data center scale under software-defined control [2], [34], and Sirius to nanosecond switching [35]. An earlier system, Helios, paired electrical packet switching with optical circuit switching in modular data centers and reconfigured the circuits as traffic shifted [36]. Other work ties the topology to the training job. TopoOpt optimizes the topology together with the parallelization strategy [37], and MixNet exploits the locality of expert parallelism in MoE training, beating topology optimizer by 1.5 and 1.3 in its reported comparisons [5]. For scheduling, circuit switches classically use Birkhoffvon Neumann (BvN) decomposition [38], which meets the busiest-port lower bound on the makespan, the total time the schedule holds its circuits, but does so by splitting demands across as many as (P 1)2 +1 configurations for ports, each paying reconfiguration delay. Faster heuristics, such as MixNets greedy reconfiguration [5], state no worst-case bound. Research schedulers model the cost of switching explicitly. Solstice schedules hybrid circuit and packet switches by heuristic and lands within 14% of optimal at scale, without worst-case bound [39]. Eclipse carries constant-factor guarantee on the traffic circuit switch serves within fixed time window [40], and Sunflow finishes coflow, group of flows that completes together, within 2 of the optimal time [41]. Solstice and Eclipse halt the whole switch for delay δ at every change of configuration, and Sunflow halts only the ports being reconfigured. Work from 2025 and 2026 schedules circuit switches for machine-learning jobs specifically. Chronos derives circuit schedules ahead of time from the training program, leaving expert parallelism as the one pattern it must schedule on demand [42]. Spectra schedules one AI demand matrix across parallel circuit switches with the reconfiguration delay in the objective [43], LACE and Flux compile reconfiguration schedules from the structure of the whole workload [44], [45], DELTA engineers one static topology from the jobs dependency graph [46], OMLSched schedules jobs on optical ML clusters [47], and Silverstone reconfigures the fabric across the phases of disaggregated RL [48]. Amponsah and Addanki show that the many matchings of BvN decomposition fragment MoE execution into small batches [49]. Coflow schedulers for parallel and multi-core circuit switches now carry worst-case guarantees with the reconfiguration delay in the model [50], [51]; Chens makespan ratio grows with the number of flows at port. Section IV-IV-B sets out how the decomposition works, what it costs, and how FoldFits bound compares with these. c) Microring stabilization and module reliability: microring modulator responds to light only near one particular wavelength, its resonance, and that wavelength moves with temperature. standard 220-nm silicon rings resonance shifts about 77 pm/C near 1550 nm [52], and our model uses 70 pm/C as representative value. In NVIDIAs design the lasers that feed it sit in temperature-controlled module [9], so it is the rings drift, not the lasers, that the link must track. Once ring drifts past the largest offset the receiver tolerates, the receiver loses lock on it. Parts in the field stabilize the ring by reactive dither locking: the controller varies the rings setting slightly and reads how the output responds. That response shows which way the resonance has moved, so the correction comes only after an offset has appeared. ring reacquires lock in roughly 200 µs [53], and its link carries nothing until it does. Integrated thermal stabilization of individual microring modulators has also been demonstrated in hardware [54], modelpredictive and feedforward control of microring modulators has been designed in simulation [55], and locking driven by the bit error rate now tracks 71.4 nm/s with no measurable error-rate penalty under 40 disturbance [56]. Closest to ThermaLead, Yoon et al. show that the compute bursts of MoE training heat wafer-scale optical interconnect by several kelvin within milliseconds and stall its rings unless the heater is pre-driven from GPU kernel launches or the tracking loop runs much faster [57]. ThermaLead instead forecasts the drift from temperature telemetry. Lumentum has demonstrated two external laser modules delivering 16 channels on 200 GHz grid at about 24 dBm per channel [58], and Sirius-class tunable lasers switch within 912 ps [35]. However, the open issue for the laser modules is reliability: how many spare lasers pool must hold. In [59], it was showed that an integrated laser, which cannot be cooled and runs at the 70 maximum chip temperature, needs backup laser to meet 1% annual failure-rate target, whereas an external source can be cooled by thermoelectric cooler [59]. Pooling needs far fewer spares than backup per laser: tunablelaser sparing restores 32-wavelength link with only 48 shared spares under moderate load [21]. Neither analysis models correlated laser failures, so both correspond to the zero-correlation case, ρ 0, to which the coverage model of Section IV-IV-A reduces. Studies of distributed storage show the cost of that omission. In Googles storage fleet, failing to model correlated node failures typically overestimated availability by at least two orders of magnitude [60], and random replica placement is almost guaranteed to lose data when cluster-wide power outage takes many nodes down at once [61]. We found no published vendor pool-sizing rule with coverage guarantee. d) Formal tools: Coverage bounds, the MULTIFIT packing ratios of Section IV-IV-B, one-step-ahead prediction, and threshold protection are the four formal tools this paper builds on. All four have long record in optical WDM survivability and scheduling [17][21]. That work targeted fiber cuts at gigabit rates. The AI data center adds correlated thermal stress on shared laser pools and on microrings running at 200 Gb/s per lane, and each component here is designed anew for that setting. III. LASER POOLING: THE CORRELATION CEILING Pooling spares works like insurance, and it fails for the same reason. Ten thousand houses in different towns burn independently, so small reserve covers the years claims. Ten thousand houses on one floodplain produce every claim in single flood, and insuring more houses there adds exposure without diversifying it. Co-packaged lasers that share cooling and power resemble the floodplain: one shared cause can bring burst of failures that overwhelms spares sized for scattered ones. A. Mathematical Model Definitions: We need to know whether the spares in pool cover the lasers that fail in window. Consider pool of lasers whose failures are exchangeable, meaning that no laser is special: any set of lasers is as likely to be the failing set as any other. Failures are counted over fixed window of time: is the number that fail in one window, and = F/N is the failure fraction. The window is the restock interval, the time pool runs before its failed modules are replaced and its spares refilled, and every coverage and availability figure in this paper is per-window quantity. One lasers probability of failing during one window is its marginal failure probability λ, which later sections also call its per-window failure rate, so λ = 0.05 means one-in-twenty chance per laser per window. Laser reliability is usually quoted as FIT rate, failures per 109 device hours, and laser at φ FIT with window of tw hours has λ = 1 exp(φ tw 109). The failure correlation ρ (0, 1), the pairwise (intraclass) correlation between failures, measures how strongly failures cluster. As ρ 0 the failures become independent. larger ρ means that greater share of failures traces to one cause acting on many lasers at once. Against those failures the pool holds spare lasers, giving spare ratio σ = s/N . Deployments cap the ratio, and we write the budget cap as σmax; the cap assumed throughout is the 2 pool, in which spares equal active lasers. The severity of the shared cause varies from window to window, and we model it with the beta distribution whose mean is λ and whose intraclass correlation is ρ. Analysis The theorem supplies no value for λ or ρ, and every number below moves with both. The analysis takes stress operating point of λ = 0.05 and ρ = 0.15. When the perlaser failure probability is small, ρ is the common-cause beta factor of reliability engineering: the share of failures that trace back to single shared cause. Other industries have estimated it. IEC 61508-6 assigns values from 0.005 to 0.05 for programmable electronics and from 0.01 to 0.10 for field equipment, according to the defenses in place [12], and nuclear practice uses 0.05 to 0.10 for redundant pair [11], [62]. Where the units share one die, IEC 61508-2 starts from 0.33 and accepts the redundancy as adequately separated only once the estimate is shown to be below 0.25 [63]. Lasers in one module have little physical separation, since they share its enclosure and temperature control and often Fig. 2. FoldFit: Scheduling the Circuit Switch FoldFit schedules the OCS that joins the photonic engines to one another. The switch holds only limited set of connections at time, so communication phase is served as sequence of configurations, each held for while before the switch is reconfigured. good sequence is short, because the collective waits while each configuration is held, and stable, because every reconfiguration costs switching time. FoldFit chooses the sequence by recasting the problem as packing: each traffic demand becomes job, and the jobs are packed onto the parallel circuits the switch can hold at once. The fabric is single-stage OCS with crossbar semantics. At any moment it holds one configuration, set of port-disjoint circuits, meaning that no two of them share switch port. Traffic between two engines flows only while circuit connects them, so serving workload means choosing sequence of configurations and dwell time for each. Those dwells sum to the makespan of Section II-II-B. Each change of configuration also costs fixed switching delay δ, which the makespan as defined here leaves out. The input is the demand matrix D, with entry Dij the traffic engine must send to engine j, expressed in time slots at the per-channel capacity C. The classical way to choose that sequence is the BvN decomposition [38], which pads the demand matrix until every row and column sums to the busiest ports load and writes it as weighted sum of permutation matrices, each configuration whose weight is its dwell. The dwells then meet the busiest-port bound, but over as many as (P 1)2 + 1 configurations for ports, most with tiny dwells, each costing reconfiguration delay that nothing in the decomposition bounds. FoldFit replaces the decomposition with packing, problem that has carried worst-case makespan bound since the 1970s. FoldFit treats each nonzero demand as an indivisible job of length Dij slots and the fabric as identical service channels, where is the number of port-disjoint circuits one configuration can sustain. These channels are the parallel machines of the packing problem, not the wavelength channels of the laser pool. The target is OPT, the shortest schedule that serves all jobs on parallel channels without two circuits 10 sharing port at the same time. Dropping the port condition leaves the classical makespan problem, whose optimum is no longer. Three lower bounds on that optimum are immediate. No schedule beats the largest single demand; none beats the average load (cid:80) ij Dij/m; and none beats the busiest ports total traffic, the largest row or column sum of D, because port carries one circuit at time. Starting from those bounds, Algorithm 2 binary-searches the deadline , candidate makespan, running FFD at each candidate . FFD sorts the jobs from longest to shortest and places each in turn on the first channel whose load would stay within . If every job fits, is feasible. The deadline on which the search ends fixes the assignment of jobs to channels. Binary-searched FFD is the MULTIFIT algorithm of multiprocessor scheduling, here with its search started at Tlb, and it inherits the MULTIFIT theorem. On identical channels, steps of the search give (1.22 + 2q) OPT [67], and Yue tightened the constant to the exact ratio, (13/11 + 2q) OPT [68]. Both bounds are stated against the classical optimum, which is no longer than OPT. Every deadline at which FFD fails lies below 13/11 of the classical optimum, the search starts at Tlb OPT, and its upper end, max{Tlb, (cid:80) D/m + max D}, keeps the search interval no wider than the classical optimum, so both ratios hold against OPT. They need not hold against the classical optimum itself, which the busiest-port bound can exceed several times over. With five or more steps Yues guarantee sits below 11/9, the figure we quote throughout. MULTIFIT is result about identical machines, and it applies to switch under three conditions. First, the channels have to be interchangeable, which holds while every circuit runs at the same per-channel capacity C. Second, each demand has to be packed as one indivisible job on one channel. Third, FFDs assignment of jobs to channels has to be realizable as sequence of port-disjoint configurations. The classical setting does not supply the third condition, because two jobs sitting on different channels may share switch port, and no configuration can run both at once. We call the step that turns the assignment into port-disjoint configurations the alignment. The busiest-port bound is necessary for an alignment to exist at all, which is why the binary search starts no lower than it. When demand may be split at configuration boundary, which is the relaxation BvN works in, the alignment is exact and the 11/9 guarantee carries over untouched. When demands are strictly unsplittable, the alignment can leave idle gaps that the 11/9 bound does not account for, and the worked example below loses one slot this way. On the workloads swept in Section V-V-F, FoldFits makespan lands within 6% of the larger of the first two lower bounds above on every instance, and within about 1% on average from 16 engines up. ThermaLead: Steadying the Microring The receiver loses lock once the rings resonance offset exceeds the lock threshold, the largest offset it tolerates. Parts in the field use the reactive dither locking of Section II-II-B, which corrects an offset only after observing it, so the receiver absorbs each steps drift before the correction lands. ThermaLead adds feedforward term. It predicts the next-step drift from short history and pre-positions the heater one step early, so the receiver sees only the error of that forecast. The heater and its authority are the same in both schemes; only the excursion, the swing of the offset at the receiver, changes. TriageGuard: Protecting the Modules fixed budget of hot spares cannot protect every module, so the budget should go to the modules most likely to fail. Deployed systems hand out spares uniformly from the shared pool. TriageGuard scores each module on its temperature, its age, and its observed forward-error-correction (FEC) bin, the band of corrected-error counts the link reports. The result is the modules risk score, the estimate of how likely it is to fail. It then pre-spares every module above risk threshold τ , up to the pre-spare budget B, the number of modules that can hold hot spare, and routes the rest to the shared pool. Protecting the top-B risks is optimal, by an exchange argument. The expected number of protected failures is additive over the protected set, sum of one term per protected module. Swapping protected low-risk module for an unprotected higher-risk one never lowers the sum, and repeating such swaps turns any selection into the top-B selection. Greedy top-B selection is therefore exactly optimal for any fixed risk estimate. The argument settles how to spend the budget once the modules are ranked and says nothing about whether the ranking is right, so optimality is conditional on the risk estimate, and the freshness of that estimate dominates the result below. Algorithm 4 links ranking quality to recovery time. failure on pre-spared module switches to its hot spare in tsw = 5 ms, while failure anywhere else draws from the shared pool at tmiss = 150 ms. Call the share of expected failure probability that lands on protected modules the intercepted mass µ. The mean time to recover (MTTR) is µ tsw + (1 µ) tmiss, so MTTR falls linearly as the ranking intercepts more of the mass. Uniform sparing of modules out of intercepts B/M of it on average, and risk ranking improves on that only as far as it aims at the modules that will fail. The all-dynamic baseline, in which every failure draws from the shared pool, bounds the MTTR of any ranking from above, because protected failure can only shorten repair. The one infeasible corner asks for 500 counts at 0.6 times the nominal gain, more than the 480 the plant reaches at full duty, and there the servo 19 correctly holds the duty at 255 and the integral at its cap. Its phase and gain margins stay at or above 22.5 and 14.9 dB across the sweep, and an independent recomputation confirms them. The swept plant time constants include the 30.9 µs and 0.71 ms of measured microring heater [77] and the 13.8 µs of metal microheater [78]; doped-silicon microheaters, at 0.98 µs [78], are faster than the sweep covers. C. Packaging The fallback can be built from catalog silicon with an ordinary pinout: the iCE40UP5K in the 48-pad SG48 package. The interface brought out to the package is deliberately narrow  (Fig. 18)  . deployed part would carry setpoints and telemetry to the supervisory host one level above this device over management bus such as I2C, in place of the two-pin serial test port, and the wide data buses stay on chip behind that serial test harness. Placed together with the harness, the design occupies 202 of the 5,280 logic cells, or 3.83%, against the 2.52% that synthesis counts for the core alone. To test whether one device can serve several thermal domains, we placed and routed eight instances of the core without the shared telemetry bus that would report them to the supervisory host. They occupy 1,417 of the 5,280 logic cells (26.8%) and close timing on all six seeds under both models, at 55.2558.59 MHz under nextpnr and 55.9158.92 MHz under icetime; the bus itself has not been placed. Both safety-critical circuits are placed and routed for shipping part, close timing under the place-and-route tool on every seed, and use very little area, and the bypass is proven property of their register-transfer design, so the fallback path can be built. Whether Halley then delivers the reliability outcome still depends on the unmeasured correlation ρ of Section III, which only the field measurement of Section VII-VII-E would settle. VII. DISCUSSION A. Impact on Capital and Power Costs The goodput gain of Section V-V-D is an upper bound on the useful compute, and so the capital, that Halley frees. The coverage reading multiplies the useful compute the same hardware delivers by up to 1.17, 17.3% rise, and the litshare reading by up to 1.03. Both factors hold only if fabric stall is the sole recoverable loss, and it is not. Model FLOPs utilization (MFU), the share of peak arithmetic that training run keeps busy, also counts compute, memory, pipeline-bubble, and data-loading losses that the control plane never touches. The 65.2% goodput here and the 3843% MFU that Llama 3 reported therefore do not conflict. At that bound, the gain cuts the accelerators, capital, and provisioned power needed for given training output by up to 14.7%, or 3.3% on the lit-share reading, for fixed rack design and power-smoothing scheme. Energy falls by less, because accelerators waiting at barrier draw less than full power [23]. Where power and local approval limit new AI data centers (Section I), the gain becomes more training from existing sites instead of saving. It is one-time factor on top of the 30 to 40% yearly improvement in accelerator performance per the alternative, and each point of availability recovers training time in proportion to the attribution fraction. The second is the tail-latency objective of MoE inference. Generating token runs the same all-to-all exchange as training; that exchange takes 3040% of iteration time in DeepSeek-V3 training on H100 before overlap with computation and under 5% after [22]. If decoding falls in the same range, FoldFits 11/9 bound caps the worst-case inflation of an iteration, under its stated conditions, at 6.78.9% before switching delay and with circuits held across steps, or at about 1% once the exchange is overlapped. The third is capacity planning before ρ is measured. Observation 2 shows that decorrelating first is the cheaper path across the plausible band, and the coupled model plans against the goodput tail that the independent model hides. The fourth is the control interface. The algorithms are cheap and step aside on flagged forecast, so apart from ThermaLeads forecast (Section VII-VII-D) the obstacle to deployment is an interface that exists only in part. External laser modules report per-lane bias, power, and alarms and accept per-lane enable [79], and commercial optical circuit switches expose NETCONF and RESTCONF control [80]. Neither the OIF management framework for co-packaged engines nor the ELSFP interface, however, defines per-ring temperature or lock state [79], [81]. One change would unblock both deployment and the field measurement of ρ (Section VII-VII-E): published interface exposing per-laser health and failure timestamps, perring temperature and lock state, and switch reconfiguration hooks on the management interface the packages already carry. C. Impact on Inference, Post-Training, and RL Traffic Halley was developed for training, where the failure data of Section II show the need. The same fabric now carries inference and RL as well, but of the four components only FoldFit carries guarantee that transfers cleanly. FoldFit transfers: MoE decoding runs the same all-to-all expert dispatch on its critical path when experts are spread across the fabric. Serving that disaggregates attention from the experts sends M-to-N traffic instead [82]. On inference-shaped demand, across expert-parallel degrees from 8 to 128 and packed without the port condition, the schedule stays within 1% of the classical lower bound and never exceeds 11/9, so the same cap on worst-case iteration inflation, before switching delay, applies across that sweep. RL post-training inherits the result through rollout, which is inference and takes from half to over 90% of the step in reported systems [83][85]; by Amdahls law, hypothetical 10% rollout speed-up would be roughly 5 to 9% step speed-up. Weight synchronization between phases is separate load: under 1.6 for 72B model inside one cluster, against rollouts of hundreds to thousands of seconds [86], but enough to stall rollouts at terabyte scale, especially across data centers [87]. Availability and thermal are training-first: Reported machine failures run about 13.6 lower per thousand machines per week for an inference service than for pretraining at scale, 2.2 against 30 [88]. If the per-laser rate fell by the same factor, the same coverage bound would put fixed four-laser Fig. 18. The device, the placement, and the pins, in the iCE40 and 130 nm builds. Scaled by it, the coverage readings 17.3% rise becomes 13.0%, 8.6%, and 5.8% at three-quarters, half, and third, and the lit-share readings rise becomes 2.5%, 1.7%, and 1.1%. Llama 3 gives the fraction scale. tenth of its 419 unexpected interruptions were traced to network switches, cables, and interface cards [23], which would put the gain near 1.7% on the coverage reading and 0.3% on the lit-share reading. That breakdown counts interruptions, not stalled time, so it gives scale rather than value, and this work does not measure the fraction for co-packaged fabric. B. Addressing Practical System Losses

sections.title: The results bear on four problems that operators pay for
sections.content: today and that deployed systems leave open. The first is time lost at the synchronization barrier in hyperscale pretraining. Llama 3 held effective training time above 90% through its 419 interruptions [23]. Laser-pool exhaustion would add to that loss on co-packaged fabric, and within budget cap Theorem 1 shows that more spares alone cannot remove it. Decorrelation with fast recovery is 21 reserve at 99.1% availability, against 86.3% at the stress training rate. The machinery pays off most where failures are frequent and correlated, so we claim no per-component inference win for LightReserve, ThermaLead, or TriageGuard. The case is strongest on the largest jobs, since mean time to failure falls as the GPU count rises [27]; at platform scale, ByteDance logged 38,236 explicit and 5,948 implicit failures across 778,135 training jobs in three months [89]. Disaggregated serving also moves the key-value cache from prefill to decode over the fabric [90], [91], load that grows with context. No component removes it, and we claim no guarantee for it. D. Limitations and Open Problems The fallback rule of Section IV covers the cases it can detect: on stale, low-confidence, or late signal, the component bypasses itself. It does not catch confident but wrong forecast, on which controller can reconfigure the fabric more often than it should. Gating reconfiguration on confidence and feasibility curbs that churn without eliminating it, and formal bound on the harm is left to future work. Acting also costs compute for the predictions and energy for the heaters, and spoofed telemetry could force mis-reconfiguration, so the control interface has to be hardened. Every numerical result outside Section VI is calibrated simulation or closed-form evaluation, and those of Section VI are synthesis, place-and-route, signoff, and proof outputs, which settle the logic and its static timing but leave the process and interfaces to fabrication; none is measurement on hardware. The two loss shares of the goodput model are assumptions, and most of the stress-point gain comes from provisioning the spare lasers that the coverage bound sizes (Section V-V-D). Six limits bound the claims. First, the failure inputs are assumed: the correlation ρ, on which both the sparing result and the ceiling depend, and the per-laser failure rate, for which we found no published field value for the lasers inside external laser modules. The headline figures use the stress setting λ = 0.05 per window, and 99.999% stays out of reach inside the 2 cap of the 32-channel pool only while λ exceeds about 2.4 104 (Table II). We anchor ρ in the common-cause beta factors of Section III-III-B but cannot yet calibrate it to field data for these laser form factors, so the recommendation rests on the sweep of Observation 2. Second, of the three conditions that carry FoldFits 11/9 guarantee onto switch (Section IV-IV-B), two hold by construction here. The third, realizing the packing as portdisjoint configurations, is exact only when demand may be split at configuration boundary and resumed later, and proof for demands that must each run on one uninterrupted circuit is open. The guarantee also covers dwell time only, not the switching delay of each reconfiguration. Third, ThermaLeads moving-average forecast does slightly worse than the dither lock on the stress trace of Section IV-IV-C, and in the released sweep its deficit grows to 4967% when the heat cycles phase jumps randomly every 16 steps or more often, and to 17% under random temperature steps of 1 standard deviation every 4 steps. Gated, both deficits stay within 4.3%, an empirical limit, not proof. deployable ThermaLead needs forecast matched to the drift and aware of regime changes. Comparisons with the fastest reactive loops now reported [56] and with heater pre-driving from kernel launches [57] remain open, since both need the control step in seconds, which the per-step analysis leaves free. Fourth, several external anchors are vendor-reported or forward-looking, and each is hedged where it appears. Fifth, Proposition 1 covers only the correlation-driven part of goodput, and Section V-V-E states what genuine floor under realized goodput would also require. Sixth, the composed goodput turns on what spare shortfall costs real job, and the two readings of Section V-V-D are cases, not bounds. E. The Measurement That Turns the Bound into Forecast Theorem 1 bounds availability in terms of ρ, so fleetscale measurement of that correlation would pin down the value on which the bound depends, and the measurement needs only instrumentation. Log the failure timestamp of every laser across many identical pools, count how many lasers fail together in each restock window, and estimate ρ from how far that count is over-dispersed, that is, how much more it varies than the independent-binomial expectation. Randomeffects lifetime models, which already estimate location-driven correlation from GPU fleet failure data [92], offer one way to do it. Correlated failures are rare, so credible estimate needs exposure on the order of thousands of pool-years, from hyperscaler instrumenting its own packages or vendor publishing co-failure statistics. Two choices sharpen the result. Logging the candidate shared causes lets ρ be attributed to mechanism. The full per-window distribution should also be reported, because Part (2) of Theorem 1 and Proposition 1 show that coverage and the goodput tail depend on the tail of Θ, not only on its variance. Until such data exists, ρ = 0.15 should be read as prior, and the design should rest on the full ρ-sweep. Cheaper measurements would narrow other unmeasured inputs: one instrumented package would ground the two composition loss shares, and one real job would establish both the fabrics share of recoverable stall and what spare shortfall costs it. VIII. CONCLUSIONS This paper argues that each of the four optical layers can be run step ahead of failure. Halley puts one predictive controller over each of them, though ThermaLeads simple forecast paid off mainly on smoother drift; its gate kept it near the dither lock elsewhere. Each controller steps aside when its forecast is flagged stale or unsure, so for such forecast the worst case is the reactive system it replaces; confident but wrong forecast has no such floor yet (Section VII-VII-D). One theorem shapes the design: correlated laser failures put ceiling on the coverage large pool can reach within deployable budget cap. For 32-channel pool at ρ = 0.15, 99.999% stays out of reach within the 2 cap whenever lasers failure probability per restock window exceeds about 2.4 104, as it does for laser at the 50 FIT source target restocked once year. Between that target and the stress level, correlation raises the spares that 99.999% takes more than tenfold. That target is then reached by decorrelating the pool first and sizing the spares against the correlation that remains. Under the stated cost model, that path costs $44,100 at the stress operating point against $234,000 for the pure-spares alternative, 5.3 saving, and it stays the cheaper of the two across the whole plausible band of ρ, which the field has not yet measured. Composed from the simulated components, effective cluster goodput at the stress operating point rose 11.3 points on the coverage reading and 2.2 points on the lit-share reading. Most of the first figure comes from the larger spare pool, and holding it to the 2 cap leaves 11.1 points. The margin over todays reactive stack is narrowest under mild conditions, about 1.3% in relative terms at 50 FIT. How much of that gain real job would keep depends on the fabrics share of recoverable stall, which this work did not measure. The part of the gain that job keeps reduces the accelerators and megawatts its training needs, by up to 3.314.7% at the stress operating point. That much data center capacity need not be built. The fallback that early action relies on is synthesized, placed and routed for shipping FPGA and passes signoff as 130 nm layout, and its combined core is machine-proven to match an independent specification core on every cycle. An operator should size the pool from measured failure rate and measured correlation, spend the next dollar on separating the lasers before buying more of them, and plan capacity against bad window such as the fifth percentile. Further research can help realize deployed system. What remains open, ThermaLeads forecast and the theory, is stated in Section VII-VII-D. Running these controllers on real optics needs the parts of the telemetry and actuation interface that the optics vendors have not yet published, chiefly perring temperature and lock state. Estimating ρ across fleet needs only enough pools instrumented for long enough. This measurement would turn the ceiling proved here from bound conditioned on an assumed correlation into forecast.
